title: Why $9.99 Tricks Your Brain
voiceover: Why does $9.99 feel so much cheaper? It's called the left-digit effect. Your brain reads numbers left to right and anchors on the first digit. So $9.99 gets filed as 'about nine dollars' while $10 gets filed as 'ten dollars', even though the gap is one cent. Researchers Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz found that a one-cent drop feels bigger when it changes the first digit, like $3.00 to $2.99. Stores know this, which is why so many prices end in nine. The effect varies by product, and round prices can signal quality for premium brands. So when you see a price ending in nine, mentally round up before deciding. Ask yourself: would I buy this at ten? You'll spot it everywhere. Tomorrow: the reason your brain quietly ignores facts you disagree with.

description: Why does $9.99 feel so much cheaper than $10? Your brain anchors on the leftmost digit, so a one-cent change can feel like a much bigger drop. Source: Thomas & Morwitz (2005), 'Penny wise and pound foolish: the left-digit effect in price cognition', Journal of Consumer Research.
accuracy_note: The left-digit effect is well documented, but its strength depends on the product and context. Premium or luxury brands often use round prices because round numbers can signal quality.
